name: Times Literary Supplement cryptic crossword No 1,173

solutions.check: grid rebuilt from the blog's light list (unique); every answer written into it with each crossing agreeing

clue.text: Liszt, for instance, putting notes together

indicators.note: things placed together are joined side by side, so single letters are strung into one word

blocks.note: four musical notes, each named by a letter from A to G

explanation.surface: Liszt at the piano, gathering notes into a composition.
explanation.walkthrough: Liszt took minor orders late in life and was known as the Abbé Liszt; the four letters are also all note names.
explanation.definitionFit: An abbé is a French title for a cleric, and Liszt took holy orders in Rome in 1865.

clue.text: Group of rhymes in Petrarchan sonnet

blocks.note: first meaning: the Swedish pop group
second meaning: the rhyme scheme of each quatrain in the octave of an Italian sonnet

explanation.surface: A literature student noting which lines rhyme in a Petrarchan sonnet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Group of rhymes' reads as one phrase; split it, and 'Group' is the band while the rhymes are the scheme.
explanation.definitionFit: The Petrarchan octave rhymes in the pattern ABBAABBA, and the same four letters name the famous Swedish band.

clue.text: Composer sounding like 6

indicators.note: a thing that sounds like another is said the same way, so the spoken form matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: the answer to 6 Down, a minor Dickens character

explanation.surface: A composer whose name sounds like something else.
explanation.walkthrough: The two long down entries are clued by each other: same sound, different last syllable spellings.
explanation.definitionFit: Britten was the leading English composer of the twentieth century, writer of Peter Grimes and the War Requiem.

clue.text: Credited to Alexander Scriabin initially then heartlessly copied

indicators.note: initially means at the start, so only the opening letters of the named words are used
without a heart, a word loses its central letter
then means next in order, so one part follows another

blocks.note: the composer's initials
to crib is to copy someone else's work

explanation.surface: A disputed manuscript attributed to Scriabin turns out to have been plagiarised.
explanation.walkthrough: Cribbed has seven letters, so its heart is the fourth, one of the two Bs.
explanation.definitionFit: To ascribe a work to someone is to attribute it, so ascribed to means credited to as author.

clue.text: Look, it’s about rising maestro

indicators.note: about means around, so one piece wraps the other
in a down entry, rising means read from the bottom up

blocks.note: taken as written, dropping the apostrophe
lo is an old word for look or behold

explanation.surface: Someone pointing out a conductor whose career is on the up.
explanation.walkthrough: The comma after 'Look' hides that it is a piece, not an exclamation.
explanation.definitionFit: Sir Georg Solti was a celebrated Hungarian-British conductor, and maestro is the honorific for a great conductor.

clue.text: Briefly slowing down from current tempo at end of Bruckner

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: the composer's final letter
I is the physics symbol for electric current
the first letter of the word, as in score shorthand

explanation.surface: A conductor easing off the pace at the close of a Bruckner symphony.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Briefly' signals an abbreviated answer, the short form musicians write in a score.
explanation.definitionFit: Rit. is the score abbreviation for ritardando, the Italian instruction to slow down gradually.

clue.text: Dickensian sounding like 2

definitions.note: an adjective standing for a noun: a Dickens character

indicators.note: a thing that sounds like another is said the same way, so the spoken form matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: the answer to 2 Down, the English composer

explanation.surface: A Dickens figure whose name echoes another famous one.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue mirrors 2 Down: the Dickens character's name is pronounced just like the composer's.
explanation.definitionFit: Benjamin Britain, called Little Britain, is the manservant in Dickens's Christmas book The Battle of Life.

clue.text: Trade ideas about “What Every Woman wants”

indicators.note: to bring something about is to turn it around, so these letters are rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: People swapping views on the question of what women want.
explanation.walkthrough: The quoted phrase echoes J. M. Barrie's play What Every Woman Knows, which disguises it as a title.
explanation.definitionFit: Desiderata are things desired or needed, the Latin plural for wishes, so it means the things someone wants.

clue.text: John Reid, some say, permanently associated with Rossini’s music

definitions.text: John Reid, some say, permanently associated with Rossini’s music

blocks.note: reads like a real person with a disputed reputation; in some versions of the story it is the masked hero's real name
the William Tell Overture became the radio and television theme for this western hero

explanation.walkthrough: John Reid sounds like a politician or music manager; he is the Texas Ranger who survived an ambush and became a masked hero.
explanation.definitionFit: The galloping finale of Rossini's William Tell Overture is so tied to the masked western hero that many know it only as his theme.

clue.text: “We got to … Heidelberg before the night –” (Mark Twain)

definitions.text: “We got to … Heidelberg before the night –” (Mark Twain)

blocks.clueFragment: “We got to … Heidelberg before the night –”
blocks.note: a line of prose with a gap at its end, which the missing verb fills
the source points to Twain's travel book A Tramp Abroad

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue: Twain describes reaching Heidelberg just as darkness fell.
explanation.definitionFit: Night is said to close in or come down on a place, and the two-word phrase completes Twain's sentence.

clue.text: Waltzing Matilda composer’s instrument

blocks.note: first meaning: the nickname of Andrew Paterson, who wrote the words of the Australian song
second meaning: a plucked stringed instrument with a round drum-like body

explanation.surface: Asking what the author of Waltzing Matilda played.
explanation.walkthrough: The possessive makes it look as though one should name an instrument he played; instead the pen name and the instrument are the same word.
explanation.definitionFit: Andrew 'Banjo' Paterson, Australian poet, wrote Waltzing Matilda; a banjo is a plucked string instrument with a drum-like body.

clue.text: Intervals, e.g. B to C, arranged in the sol-fa, I omitted

indicators.note: to arrange is to put into a new order, so these letters are reshuffled
something omitted is left out, so the named letter is dropped

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written, without the hyphen
the letter to be removed

explanation.surface: A theory lesson on semitones taught through the sol-fa system.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' looks like a link word but is part of the material, losing its I.
explanation.definitionFit: A half tone, or semitone, is the smallest interval in Western music, such as the step from B up to C.

clue.text: One born near Rome – an Italian composer – not Monaco, not I, that’s all wrong

indicators.note: not means without, so the named letters are taken away
something all wrong is in disorder, so what remains is rearranged

blocks.note: taken as written
letters to be removed
a further letter to be removed

explanation.surface: Identifying an Italian composer born near Rome while ruling out someone from Monaco.
explanation.walkthrough: 'an Italian composer' reads as part of the definition, but it is the raw material; the composer's name is also his birthplace's.
explanation.definitionFit: Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina took his name from the hill town of Palestrina, east of Rome, where he was born.

clue.text: Sinfonia by VW includes start of coda in large-scale mass

indicators.note: to include is to hold within, so one piece sits inside the other
the start of a word is its first letter, so only that letter is kept

blocks.note: Vaughan Williams's Seventh Symphony is Sinfonia Antartica, spelt the Italian way
the first letter of the word

explanation.surface: A symphony by Vaughan Williams with a big coda performed on a massive scale.
explanation.walkthrough: VW is Ralph Vaughan Williams; his symphony title lacks a C, which the coda supplies. 'Mass' looks musical but is a landmass.
explanation.definitionFit: Antarctica is a continent, an enormous landmass covered in ice around the South Pole.

clue.text: Help! is rendered without Beatles’ finale

indicators.note: a finale is the closing part, so only the last letter is taken
without means lacking, so a letter is removed

blocks.note: a line rendered by an actor is said, delivered aloud in performance
the last letter of the band's name

explanation.surface: The Beatles' song Help! performed without its closing chord.
explanation.walkthrough: Help! is a Beatles title, which makes the definition look like part of the story.
explanation.definitionFit: Aid is assistance, so the cry for assistance can be replaced by the noun meaning support.

clue.text: Work that comes after The Siege and Fall of Troy?

definitions.text: comes after The Siege and Fall of Troy?

blocks.note: first meaning: a job or profession

blocks.clueFragment: comes after The Siege and Fall of Troy?
blocks.note: second meaning: what follows a city's capture, when the victors hold it

explanation.surface: Asking what book or opus followed a work about the fall of Troy.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Work' and the title suggest a sequel; the question mark flags that the second meaning is military, not literary.
explanation.definitionFit: Occupation means employment, and also the holding of captured territory by an army after a siege succeeds.

clue.text: Musical regarded as elegant at one time

blocks.note: chic means stylish
ago means in the past

explanation.surface: A show that was once thought stylish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Musical' looks like an adjective describing something elegant, but it is the noun: a stage show.
explanation.definitionFit: Chicago is the Kander and Ebb stage musical about jazz-age murderesses, later an Oscar-winning film.

clue.text: Tone row about start of toccata featuring more staccato notes …

indicators.note: the start of a word is its first letter, so only that is used
about means around, so the outer pieces enclose another

blocks.note: do or doh is the first note of the sol-fa scale
the first letter of the word
a tier is a row, as of seats

explanation.surface: A twelve-tone row in a toccata written with many detached notes.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tone row' reads as Schoenberg's serial term; it splits into two pieces. Staccato is marked by dots above the notes.
explanation.definitionFit: Staccato notes are written with dots, so a score with more of them is literally more dotted, a jokey comparative of dotty.

clue.text: “The damp, — -soaked soil is sick with the teeming life of a hundred years” (Kipling)

definitions.text: “The damp, — -soaked soil is sick with the teeming life of a hundred years” (Kipling)

blocks.clueFragment: “The damp, — -soaked soil is sick with the teeming life of a hundred years”
blocks.note: a line of prose with a gap before a hyphenated adjective, which the missing word fills
the source tells the solver which author's description of an Indian city to recall

explanation.walkthrough: This is a quotation clue from Kipling's descriptions of insanitary Indian streets.
explanation.definitionFit: Drainage is waste water carried away from land or buildings, and soil soaked by it is foul and unhealthy.

clue.text: … not like Schubert’s 8th

blocks.note: reads as a comment that the previous piece differs from a famous symphony
the Unfinished Symphony, which was at least started; its opposite was never begun at all

explanation.walkthrough: The ellipsis carries on from 17 Across. Schubert's Eighth is the Unfinished, so something unlike it in the opposite direction is not even started.
explanation.definitionFit: Unbegun means not yet started, the comic contrary of a symphony left unfinished after two movements.

clue.text: One often changing position, thanks to Ahab finally with killer whale returning

indicators.note: finally points to the very end, so only the last letter is used
with means alongside, so one part is joined to the next
to return is to go back the way you came, so the string is read backwards

blocks.note: ta is informal British for thank you
the captain's final letter
orca is another name for the killer whale

explanation.surface: Ahab's quarry is a whale, so the scene is a ship tacking about in Moby-Dick.
explanation.walkthrough: The whale evokes Moby-Dick, but Ahab only lends a letter and the whale is an orca, not the white sperm whale.
explanation.definitionFit: An acrobat performs tumbles, flips and balances, constantly shifting body posture in the circus ring.

clue.text: Maupassant’s friend, given a ring, we hear

blocks.note: reads as some companion of the French writer
a ring is a bell, which sounds like Bel

explanation.surface: Someone phoning a friend of the French author.
explanation.walkthrough: Maupassant's novel Bel-Ami is about a handsome friend; put the bell in front and the friend is what is left.
explanation.definitionFit: Ami is French for friend, the second half of the title of Maupassant's 1885 novel Bel-Ami.

clue.text: Composer of tune in B, sir

indicators.note: a composer of letters puts them in order, so the following letters are made into something new

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Addressing someone about who wrote a melody in B.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Composer of' does double duty: the composer is the answer and also composes, or arranges, the letters that follow.
explanation.definitionFit: Anton Rubinstein was a Russian pianist and composer who founded the St Petersburg Conservatory.

clue.text: Librettist without appeal to show disapproval

indicators.note: without in its old sense means outside, so one piece goes round the other

blocks.note: to boo is to jeer
it is old slang for sex appeal

explanation.surface: A librettist with no charm draws jeers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'without appeal' reads as lacking charm, but without means outside here.
explanation.definitionFit: Arrigo Boito wrote the libretti for Verdi's Otello and Falstaff, so he is a famous author of opera texts.

clue.text: A feature associated with Greek thinkers from Socrates to Aristotle

definitions.text: A feature associated with Greek thinkers

indicators.note: from means taken out of, so the letters are lifted straight from the following words

blocks.note: spans the end of the first name, the small word, and the start of the second name

explanation.surface: A history of Greek philosophy from Socrates to Aristotle.
explanation.walkthrough: 'from Socrates to Aristotle' reads as a span of history.
explanation.definitionFit: A stoa is a covered colonnade; Zeno taught in the Painted Stoa at Athens, which gave the Stoics their name.

clue.text: Laying to rest Wagner’s magnum opus after a leaderless season

indicators.note: with no leader, a word loses its first letter
after means following, so one part is placed behind the other

blocks.note: one of the four seasons
Der Ring des Nibelungen, his four-opera cycle, usually called the Ring

explanation.surface: Finally finishing Wagner's huge cycle after a season with no conductor.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Laying to rest' could suggest completing a project; it is literal burial.
explanation.definitionFit: To inter is to bury a body, so interring is putting someone in the grave.

clue.text: Popular composer’s first section won’t progress if stuck in this

definitions.text: won’t progress if stuck in this
definitions.note: a clause describing the answer rather than a noun synonym

indicators.note: only the opening part is kept, so the rest of the name is cut away

blocks.note: John Rutter, the widely loved English choral composer

explanation.surface: A popular composer whose opening movement fails to develop.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is the definition: something you won't progress from if stuck in it.
explanation.definitionFit: A rut is a groove worn by wheels, and figuratively a dull routine in which one makes no headway.

clue.text: Perform in church antiphon

indicators.note: in means contained within, so the letters lie inside the following words

blocks.note: the end of the first word runs into the start of the second

explanation.surface: Singing an antiphon during a church service.
explanation.walkthrough: 'antiphon' is itself a sung form, which tempts one to treat it as the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: To chant is to sing or intone a text, a fitting way to perform in a liturgy.

clue.text: Musical compositions to set sonnet to

indicators.note: to set is to arrange, as type or music, so these letters are put in a new order

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Writing music to accompany a sonnet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set' sounds like setting words to music; here it reorders the letters, and 'to' is both link and fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A nonetto, or nonet, is a piece written for nine instruments or voices.

clue.text: Paul sounds like the mainstay of American pop

indicators.note: a thing that sounds like another is said the same, so the spoken form matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: an anchor is a mainstay, a source of stability; in a non-rhotic accent it ends like the singer's name

explanation.surface: A singer called Paul described as the backbone of American pop.
explanation.walkthrough: Paul Anka is the singer of Diana and the writer of My Way; 'Paul' points to the surname that goes with it.
explanation.definitionFit: The Canadian-born pop star Paul Anka is the famous bearer of the first name, so Paul is completed by this surname.
